title: I Am a Palestinian-American. Israeli Soldiers Occupied My Home for Weeks and Trashed It
author: andaleeb mahmoud
content:

Photo by Zain Jaafar/ AFP via Getty Images_

Late last month, Israeli soldiers broke down the doors to my family's home in
the occupied West Bank, took over the house, and didn't leave for almost three
weeks. I am a Palestinian American, a U.S. citizen. So are my children. The
occupation of my home in Palestine is deeply alarming, and the response I
received from my own government here in the United States has been profoundly
disappointing.

It started on Oct. 25, 2026, when the Israeli military invaded my family's
home in Turmus Ayya, in the northern Ramallah area of the occupied West Bank.
What happened was not simply a search or a brief military presence. Armed
soldiers forcibly entered our home, broke down our doors, including those to
our bedrooms, went through our personal belongings, rummaged through our
closets, and damaged and destroyed property throughout the house. We were in
the U.S. when this happened, but we could see them on our security cameras.
They left behind a home that had been forcibly entered, damaged, and violated
in the most personal way.

But the following day, on Oct. 26, 2026, things got worse. Returning to my
home, the soldiers arrived with a van and two military vehicles. They broke
through our front door again, tore down our security cameras, raised Israeli
flags, and proceeded to take over the house. From then until Friday, our
family home had effectively become military barracks. Israeli soldiers lived
inside our home, slept there, ate there, drank there, and used our private
property as though it belonged to them.

  
Imagine being thousands of miles away, knowing that armed soldiers from a
hostile foreign army have entered your home, destroyed your property, and
lived inside it. Imagine knowing that you couldn't simply return home; you
couldn't even safely approach the gate to your property; that armed soldiers
were occupying the place where your family should feel most secure. Imagine
that your tax dollars as an American citizen were funding the foreign army
that occupied your home and, despite your repeated requests for assistance,
the U.S. government refused to help.

Since this began, I have contacted the U.S. Embassy repeatedly for assistance
and protection as an American citizen. I have explained what happened,
communicated that armed Israeli soldiers were inside my home, and asked the
government, on behalf of my kids and me as U.S. citizens, to intervene.

The response I continued to receive was essentially the same: I was expected
to go to my property and face the armed soldiers myself.

I want to be very clear about how unacceptable that response was. They were
asking an American citizen to approach an occupied home where military
personnel who have already demonstrated a blatant disregard for human life,
who have shown willingness to break down doors, destroy property, remove
security cameras, and establish a military presence, were staying. They were
asking me to put myself and my family in a very obvious, dangerous
confrontation with armed soldiers to reclaim access to my own home.

Why should that responsibility fall on me? Why was I being told to put my own
safety at risk when I am specifically reaching out to my government for
protection and diplomatic assistance?

Late last week, my husband, Naji Abu Awad, traveled to Turmus Ayya and
attempted to speak to the soldiers outside our home. They responded by pushing
him, threatening to arrest him, and firing tear gas at my family and other
villagers and journalists who had gathered. The soldiers were armed with guns.
My husband carried an American flag and his suitcase. We did what the U.S.
government told us to do, and that's the response we got. If this is how
Israel treats us, imagine what they do to Palestinians who are not U.S.
citizens.

The soldiers finally left on Friday. They trashed my home. They spray-painted
the Star of David on our walls. My children's mattresses had been pulled off
their beds. Our sheets and comforters had been put up outside the windows.
Trash was left all over the floors. Our couch had been pulled outside on the
balcony.

We are happy that we have our home back - that the soldiers are finally gone.
But what's to stop them from raiding our home again? What about the property
they destroyed? And why did my husband have to drop everything and travel
thousands of miles, risk his safety, and be threatened with arrest to confront
the Israeli military himself? Why did the American government do nothing to
help us instead? Why is our government still doing nothing to hold Israel
accountable for the destruction it has caused and to prevent the Israeli
military from taking over our home again?

Perhaps I shouldn't be surprised that the Trump administration was less than
eager to help, given the U.S. government has done nothing to support my
community of[ Turmus
Ayya](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/03/palestinian-village-
trapped-surge-settler-violence-turmus-ayya-west-bank) - where more than 80% of
residents are U.S. citizens. Our village, where my parents were born, has been
repeatedly attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers, and the U.S. has made no
meaningful attempt to pressure Israel to stop it. Ambassador[ Mike Huckabee
did show up](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-ambassador-visits-
palestinian-town-amid-rise-west-bank-settler-violence-2026-09-05/) in
September. It was a meaningless photo op.

I'm not asking for anything unreasonable. I want accountability for the
destruction of our property, and I want our government to stop using our tax
dollars to arm and fund a military as it brutally occupies and oppresses
Palestinians.

This episode has impacted our five children the most. They were already
dealing with the trauma of having two of their friends killed by Israeli
violence since last year. Now that trauma has been compounded. My girls have
trouble eating and are worried for the safety of their father. They had been
looking forward to visiting Palestine this summer, but this experience has
turned a place they associate with safety and happiness into a source of
distress.

I am relieved the soldiers have left - and I have my house back. But I worry
that it will never truly feel like a home again - one where I feel a sense of
privacy and security; one where I don't look at my children's rooms without
seeing Israeli soldiers who occupied them; one where I can leave, lock up, and
know no one will enter it without our permission; one I can safely return to
whenever I want.
